articles.title: Prototype of Chandrayaan-5/LUPEX rover unveiled
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Chandrayaan-5/LuPEX mission is the fifth mission in the Chandrayaan series of lunar missions; JAXA, the Japanese space agency, unveiled the rover in Japan on November 25
The Japanese Space Agency, JAXA, has unveiled the prototype of the rover for the Chandrayaan-5/LUPEX (LUnar Polar EXploration) mission.

The Chandrayaan-5/LuPEX mission is the fifth mission in the Chandrayaan series of lunar missions to study the lunar volatile materials, including lunar water, in the vicinity of a Permanently Shadowed Region in the lunar South pole.
The JAXA unveiled the rover at the Chofu Aerospace Centre in Japan on November 25 and conducted a test demonstration.
The mission, which is scheduled to be launched in 2028 by the Japanese H3-24L launch vehicle, is a joint collaboration between the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the JAXA.
While the rover will be developed by the JAXA, the ISRO will be developing the lunar lander and will also be developing a few scientific instruments for the mission.

“The scientific instruments for this mission would be contributed by the ISRO, JAXA, European Space Agency (ESA) and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), all thematically connected with the exploration and in-situ analysis of the volatiles reserved in the lunar polar region,” the ISRO had earlier said.
The NASA’s Neutron Spectrometer (NS) will also be onboard the rover, and according to the Japanese space agency, it is a neutron detector designed to search for water beneath the lunar surface.
Similarly, the ESA’s Exploration Mass Spectrometer for LUPEX (EMS-L) will also be part of the mission.
The ESA said that the EMS-L would investigate the moon’s extremely thin exosphere, a tenuous mist of atoms and molecules surrounding the lunar surface.
The Chandrayaan-5/LuPEX mission received an approval from the Union government on March 10, 2025, in the form of financial sanction.

The Chandrayaan-5/LuPEX mission is the fifth mission in the Chandrayaan series of lunar missions; JAXA, the Japanese space agency, unveiled the rover in Japan on November 25

The Japanese Space Agency, JAXA, has unveiled the prototype of the rover for the Chandrayaan-5/LUPEX (LUnar Polar EXploration) mission.

The Chandrayaan-5/LuPEX mission is the fifth mission in the Chandrayaan series of lunar missions to study the lunar volatile materials, including lunar water, in the vicinity of a Permanently Shadowed Region in the lunar South pole.

The JAXA unveiled the rover at the Chofu Aerospace Centre in Japan on November 25 and conducted a test demonstration.

The mission, which is scheduled to be launched in 2028 by the Japanese H3-24L launch vehicle, is a joint collaboration between the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the JAXA.

While the rover will be developed by the JAXA, the ISRO will be developing the lunar lander and will also be developing a few scientific instruments for the mission.

“The scientific instruments for this mission would be contributed by the ISRO, JAXA, European Space Agency (ESA) and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), all thematically connected with the exploration and in-situ analysis of the volatiles reserved in the lunar polar region,” the ISRO had earlier said.

The NASA’s Neutron Spectrometer (NS) will also be onboard the rover, and according to the Japanese space agency, it is a neutron detector designed to search for water beneath the lunar surface.

Similarly, the ESA’s Exploration Mass Spectrometer for LUPEX (EMS-L) will also be part of the mission.

The ESA said that the EMS-L would investigate the moon’s extremely thin exosphere, a tenuous mist of atoms and molecules surrounding the lunar surface.

The Chandrayaan-5/LuPEX mission received an approval from the Union government on March 10, 2025, in the form of financial sanction.

articles.title: Meet Plavu Jayan, the man creating jackfruit villages across Keralam
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Jackfruit evangelist KR Jayan, winner of the 29th PV Thampy Memorial Award, reflects on his journey in conservation and his deep bond with the tree

KR Jayan’s days literally begin and end under the jackfruit tree. Having devoted 27 years of his life to its conservation, Jayan says it is only fitting that he spends all his waking hours under his beloved tree. “If you observe closely enough, you will see that the tree never sleeps — its leaves remain crisp like pappads through day and night. A seed-grown tree can live for 150 to 200 years. It is indeed very special,” he says.

Jayan, better known as Plavu Jayan (plavu is jackfruit in Malayalam), from Irinjalakkuda, Thrissur, is the recipient of the 29th PV Thampy Memorial Award 2026 for his tireless contribution to the conservation of jackfruit through the traditional method of planting.

It is a bond that goes back to his childhood, says the 61-year-old Jayan. “The jackfruit was an integral part of agrarian economy in our villages. The jackfruit was everywhere, it was an inevitable part of our lives. My mother’s family had a farming background, so my interest in jackfruit grew,” says Jayan.

The moniker Plavu Jayan came much ahead of his tree planting days. “I was 13 years old when, during Service Week in school, we were asked to get saplings. While everyone brought flowering plants, I brought a jackfruit sapling. From that day, everyone started calling me Plavu Jayan. The name stuck and I am proud of it,” he says.
Plavu Jayan at Avittathoor in Irinjalakkuda | Photo Credit: THULASI KAKKAT

In the mid nineties, as Jayan’s interest in the tree grew, he began looking for different varieties, understanding the methods of pollination and experimenting with planting. He didn’t have land of his own, so he started planting along the roadside in Irinjalakkuda.

Today, they are fully grown, massive jackfruit trees, which offer fruit and shade. The people of his village did not fully understand what Jayan was doing and often scoffed at him, but Jayan continued his effort — picking the right seeds, preparing them, sprouting and planting them. “My environmental activism has always been through my daily work,” he adds.

He has created nine plavu gramam (jackfruit villages) in Keralam — in Ernakulam, Kottayam, Palakkad and Thrissur districts. The first jackfruit village Jayan created was at Mundaya near Shoranur Railway Station. “It was a nine-and-a-half acre barren land, which is today a lush jackfruit forest on the banks of the Bharathapuzha.”

Environmental enthusiasts began seeking him out. An NRI, who had a three-and-a-half acre plot in Irinjalakkuda, approached him to create a jackfruit forest. Jayan planted 500 jackfruit saplings in 18 varieties and today, it is a thriving forest.
Plavu Jayan at the PV Thampy Memorial Award distribution ceremony in Kochi | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

articles.title: Pint of View Kochi lectures explore Keralam’s unique socio-cultural identity
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The lecture series brings the State’s historical, cultural and environmental narratives into an informal bar setting

A lecture is in progress on the warmly lit terrace bar of Niko Hotels in Kadavathra. The audience, sipping on drinks, listens in rapt attention to accomplished herpetologist Sandeep Das as he talks about a very special amphibian — the Indian purple frog. Research Associate, Department of Biotechnology, Government of India and Member of Kerala State Wildlife Board, Sandeep has been studying the ancient frog species for 15 years and shares his insights on its peculiar life and behaviour.

At the end of the session, a number of questions emerge from the audience and a lively discussion ensues. This is the Kochi chapter of Pint of View, a lecture movement that has taken over bars and pubs across the country, converting them into temporary learning hubs.
A Pint of View lecture | Photo Credit: Akkshay Lawrence
A movement that was launched in Bengaluru in 2025 by Harsh Snehanshu, Shruti Sah, and Meghna Chaudhary, it caught on in India, with a presence in over 16 cities now.

The Kochi chapter, launched in September, has hosted six lectures to enthusiastic crowds. Kochi curators Krupa Anilkumar and Kurien Philip are delighted with the response from the people and say the idea is to make knowledge accessible to the public in a fun way. “Many of us stop learning after we leave college. Though the desire to learn is present, we may still be carrying the trauma of competitive classroom environments. And that is where these lectures change the game. Hosted at bars and pubs, people are easily relaxed and therefore more receptive to new information and ways of thinking,” she says.
A Pint of View session in progress | Photo Credit: Akkshay Lawrence

The lectures so far reflect the historical, socio-cultural and environmental uniqueness of Keralam. The inaugural lecture was on 50 years of Kochi, by Johanne Binny Kuruvilla, founder of the Kochi Heritage Project, where he spoke about the unique modernity of Kochi — how it emerged and existed as a revolutionary space. “Intended for adults, the audience that we find here are largely working professionals, who are driven by the curiosity to learn. We have many regular attendees,” says Kurien.

The speakers are often senior academicians. But that does not exclude those with expertise in a subject. Musician, composer and co-founder of the performance collective, Oorali, Saji Oorali’s session explored the connection between spice trade and the music of Keralam. From the maappila paattu, which has traces of Arab influence, owing to the traders who visited the Malabar coast to European church music that introduced new instruments and traditions to South India and Malayalam hip-hop finding audiences around the world, the session was a glimpse into the history of Keralam’s music. The session also included live musical demonstrations.

Urban and ecological anthropologist, Mathew A Varghese, who is an assistant professor, School of International Relations and Politics, Mahatma Gandhi University, in his lecture, ‘The City Unfolding’ reflected on how Keralam’s urban spaces are designed, how they have transformed and how people experience and make sense of the places their inhabit.
For now, the lectures are hosted at Niko, Rocks and Brews and Vasco’s Corner.

articles.title: Bombay High Court puts road project on hold till State files report on mangrove loss, compensatory measures
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Bombay High Court directed the State to submit figures documenting tree cover, losses, and five-year survival rates before any orders are passed

The Bombay High Court has withheld permission for a road project in Mumbai until the State government submits a detailed report on measures taken to compensate for the loss of mangroves. The court also stated that ‘afforestation’ efforts must be completed before seeking clearances and that the process should not be treated as a mere formality.

A Bench comprising Chief Justice Mahesh C. Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna made these remarks while hearing a plea by the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) seeking permission to divert 0.2869 hectares of mangrove land in the Bandra-Kurla Complex area to construct an Automated Rapid Transit System covering 8.85 km.

A 2018 High Court ruling mandated court approval for developments affecting wetlands. Though the project will not require clearing mangroves, it impacts six trees, necessitating the planting of 100 trees as compensation.

Advocate Saket Mone, representing the MMRDA, argued that the Automated Rapid Transit System fulfills key connectivity needs. He added that tree planting falls under the jurisdiction of the Forest Department. In response, the Bench questioned why officials had not initiated remedial action when conceptualising the project.

Advocate General of Maharashtra Milind Sathe attributed the planting delays to a shortage of saline land, noting that saplings must be planted before the monsoon to ensure survival. However, the Bench pointed out a gap between regulators’ filings and ground reality, questioning how authorities could grant permission when rules mandate 30% tree cover.

The Court directed the State to submit figures documenting tree cover, losses, and five-year survival rates before any orders are passed. Stating that it does not oppose the project but will not proceed without full compliance, the Court posted the matter to November 30.
Mr. Mone was briefed by advocate Fatema Ansari, while Mr. Sathe was briefed by Government Pleader Onkar Chandurkar.

articles.title: Divyang SARTHI mobile app to be launched at National Parents’ Meet in Mysuru
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Mysuru to host 32nd National Parents’ Meet on November 28 and 29; over 450 participants from 25 States and Union Territories expected

The Divyang SARTHI mobile application, designed to support learning among persons with intellectual and developmental disabilities, will be launched at the inaugural session of the 32nd National Parents’ Meet to be held at the All India Institute of Speech and Hearing (AIISH), Mysuru, on Saturday and Sunday.

The two-day national meet is being organised by the National Confederation of Parents’ Organisations (PARIVAAR-NCPO), under the guidance of the National Institute for Empowerment of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities (NIEPID), in collaboration with Maulana Azad National Urdu University (MANUU), Hyderabad.

Sharing details of the event, PARIVAAR-NCPO National president Pankaj Maru said the meet would bring together more than 450 participants, including parents, members of the organisation’s national executive, rehabilitation professionals and other dignitaries from 25 States and Union Territories.

The meet, themed “From Care to Empowerment: Building Inclusive Communities Through Strong Families and Collective Action”, will deliberate on how families, institutions and parent-led organisations can work together to promote the rights, self-advocacy and participation of persons with intellectual and developmental disabilities.

The inaugural session will commence at 10 a.m. on Saturday. V. Vidyavathi, secretary, Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, Government of India, is scheduled to attend as the chief guest, while former IPS officer and former Governor of Puducherry Kiran Bedi will deliver the presidential address. NIEPID director Maj. B. V. Ramkumar and AIISH director M. Pushpavathi will also address the gathering. Dr. Maru will set the context for the deliberations.
The Divyang SARTHI application will be launched following an address by Abdul Wahid, Dean, School of Technology, MANUU.

PARIVAAR will also present the Rita Premlata Peshawaria Menon Award 2026 and the BMG Award 2026. Its annual report for 2025-26, awareness materials and a book authored by Col. V. K. Gautam will also be released.
A cultural evening showcasing the talents of persons with disabilities will be organised on Saturday.
AIISH, JSS Polytechnic for the Differently Abled, Mysuru, the Mysuru District Parents’ Association and the Inner Wheel Club of Mysuru Midtown are co-hosting the event.

articles.title: Do not confine Kanakadasa to one community, says Minister Rayaraddi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The saint-poet’s ideals and teachings continue to guide society towards achieving equality and harmony, according to the Higher Education Minister and Gadag district in-charge

The ideals and teachings of saint-poet Kanakadasa continue to guide society towards achieving equality and harmony by challenging caste discrimination, social inequality and superstitious practices, said Higher Education Minister and Gadag district in-charge Basavaraj Rayaraddi.

Speaking after inaugurating a district-level Kanakadasa Jayanti celebrations in Gadag on Friday, he said that Kanakadasa was one of the greatest philosophers and social reformers the country has produced.
Kanakadasa should not be confined to any particular caste or community, as his teachings belong to the entire country and offer guidance to all sections of society, he said.

Referring to the hierarchical social system that fostered inequality, Mr. Rayaraddi said that several saints and reformers have devoted their lives to building an egalitarian society. Kanakadasa conveyed the message of equality through the Bhakti movement. The Kanakana Kindi episode in Udupi illustrates how true devotion can transcend social barriers, he added.

Presiding over the programme, Gadag MLA H.K. Patil said that the teachings of Kanakadasa should reflect in people’s everyday lives. Birth anniversary celebrations of social reformers and prominent personalities from marginalised communities are intended to recognise their contributions and accord them social dignity, he said.
Such celebrations should go beyond ceremonial observances and serve as platforms to take the ideas of such reformers to people, he said.

Recalling Kanakadasa’s message, Kula Kula Endu Hodedadiri (Do not fight over caste), Mr. Patil said that the saint-poet advocated equality long ago. Referring to Basavanna’s teachings on mutual respect, he said that social reform is possible only when people give up discriminatory attitudes.

Expressing concern over the persistence of untouchability in rural areas despite considerable social progress, he said that the teachings of reformers should complement legal measures in creating awareness.
District president of the Karnataka Pradesh Kurubara Sangha Fakirappa Hebasur also spoke.
Achievers from various fields and students who have achieved academic excellence were felicitated.

🏛️ Political, National & Polity 📅 27 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 3 Min Read

📰 Do not confine Kanakadasa to one community, says Minister Rayaraddi

The saint-poet’s ideals and teachings continue to guide society towards achieving equality and harmony, according to the Higher Education Minister and Gadag district in-charge

The ideals and teachings of saint-poet Kanakadasa continue to guide society towards achieving equality and harmony by challenging caste discrimination, social inequality and superstitious practices, said Higher Education Minister and Gadag district in-charge Basavaraj Rayaraddi.

Speaking after inaugurating a district-level Kanakadasa Jayanti celebrations in Gadag on Friday, he said that Kanakadasa was one of the greatest philosophers and social reformers the country has produced.

Kanakadasa should not be confined to any particular caste or community, as his teachings belong to the entire country and offer guidance to all sections of society, he said.

Referring to the hierarchical social system that fostered inequality, Mr. Rayaraddi said that several saints and reformers have devoted their lives to building an egalitarian society. Kanakadasa conveyed the message of equality through the Bhakti movement. The Kanakana Kindi episode in Udupi illustrates how true devotion can transcend social barriers, he added.

Presiding over the programme, Gadag MLA H.K. Patil said that the teachings of Kanakadasa should reflect in people’s everyday lives. Birth anniversary celebrations of social reformers and prominent personalities from marginalised communities are intended to recognise their contributions and accord them social dignity, he said.

Such celebrations should go beyond ceremonial observances and serve as platforms to take the ideas of such reformers to people, he said.

Recalling Kanakadasa’s message, Kula Kula Endu Hodedadiri (Do not fight over caste), Mr. Patil said that the saint-poet advocated equality long ago. Referring to Basavanna’s teachings on mutual respect, he said that social reform is possible only when people give up discriminatory attitudes.

Expressing concern over the persistence of untouchability in rural areas despite considerable social progress, he said that the teachings of reformers should complement legal measures in creating awareness.

District president of the Karnataka Pradesh Kurubara Sangha Fakirappa Hebasur also spoke.

Achievers from various fields and students who have achieved academic excellence were felicitated.

articles.title: Telangana to provide financial assistance to 7,000 unemployed youth from EWS seeking jobs abroad
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Telangana government has introduced the Chief Minister’s Overseas Employment Scheme to provide financial assistance to unemployed youth from economically weaker families seeking jobs abroad. The scheme, to be implemented through the Telangana Overseas Manpower Company Limited (TOMCOM), envisages extending benefits to 7,000 candidates during the 2026–27 financial year.

The government issued guidelines for the scheme through G.O. No. 19, providing for a 50% subsidy on expenditure incurred towards foreign language training, visa processing and air travel, subject to specified ceilings. The initiative is aimed at helping eligible candidates overcome financial and skill-related barriers that prevent them from accessing employment opportunities overseas.

Of the 7,000 proposed beneficiaries, 5,880 will be candidates seeking direct overseas employment, while 1,120 will be those applying for jobs that require proficiency in foreign languages. The selection and categorisation of candidates will be based on their educational qualifications, vocational skills, interests and employment opportunities in destination countries.

Under the first category, candidates who can take up overseas jobs without specialised foreign language training or examinations will be eligible for a subsidy towards visa and air travel expenses. The government will consider expenditure of up to ₹1 lakh and provide 50% assistance, subject to a maximum of ₹50,000.

The second category covers candidates seeking jobs that require proficiency in the language of the destination country. Expenditure of up to ₹3.5 lakh will be considered, with the government providing 50% subsidy subject to a ceiling of ₹1.75 lakh. The assistance will cover either foreign language training or visa and air travel expenses, depending on the option chosen by the candidate.

The remaining 50% of the expenditure will have to be borne by beneficiaries. TOMCOM will coordinate with nationalised banks to facilitate loans for candidates unable to mobilise their share of the expenses.

The scheme will cover employment opportunities in 10 broad sectors, including construction and infrastructure, manufacturing, automobile, mechanical and electrical industries, electronics, transport and logistics, facility management, medical support services, hospitality and tourism, repair and maintenance, and domestic and personal services. TOMCOM will explore opportunities through partnerships with overseas recruitment agencies, bilateral arrangements and government-to-government labour agreements.

Candidates aged between 18 and 40 years will be eligible, subject to the requirements of the destination country and recruiting organisation. Applicants must be Telangana natives and should have studied from Class VI to X in the State. Those applying for jobs on the basis of ITI qualifications should have completed the course from a recognised institution in Telangana.

The scheme is open to unemployed candidates belonging to all social categories, provided their family income falls within the prescribed Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) income limit. Applicants should generally have at least two years of work experience in the relevant occupation, though exemptions may be considered depending on the work visa requirements of the destination country. They must also possess a passport with at least six months’ validity and meet the medical fitness requirements of the recruiting organisation.

Only one member of a family, as identified through the ration card, will be eligible for the subsidy. At least 33.33% of the benefits will be reserved for women and 5% for persons with disabilities. If sufficient eligible candidates are not available in these categories, the unutilised allocation can be redistributed among other eligible applicants with the approval of the State-level committee.

articles.title: The fiscal cost of cash-transfer schemes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: A social policy is often based on expected electoral gain, and is implemented without any ex ante appraisal; since cash transfers and subsidies are perpetual in nature and politically hard to reverse, such continuous commitment of financial resources demands prior evaluation and real-time monitoring to address potential shortcomings

Business Standard reported on May 13, 2026 that “Cash-transfer promises have moved from the margins of Indian election manifestos to the centre of political competition, with parties across States promising monthly or one-time payments.” Quoting a PRS Legislative Research report, it further said, “12 States are expected to spend nearly ₹1.68 trillion on unconditional cash-transfer schemes for women in 2025-26, … the outgo is roughly equivalent to 0.5 per cent of India’s GDP, compared with less than 0.2 per cent two years ago.”

The RBI report ‘State Finance: Study of State Budgets 2025-26’ reported that the total subsidy outlay increased from ₹1.87 trillion in 2018-19 to ₹4.26 trillion in 2025-26. States often implement promises from their election manifestos soon after forming the government and just before the next election, without any serious assessment of needs or financial commitments.

Conception and funding of an infrastructure project are guided by a Detailed Project Report (DPR) that specifies objectives, alternatives considered, financial and economic analysis, risk mitigation, baseline data, and success criteria. A social policy, by contrast, is often the outcome of an electoral promise or based on expected electoral gain, and is implemented without any comparable ex ante appraisal. Social policies affect human capabilities more directly than infrastructure projects.

The scarcity of public resources and their alternative uses make ex ante appraisal of social sector schemes essential. Moreover, social policies are vulnerable to electoral clientelism, and should therefore adhere to the same principles of public expenditure as infrastructure projects — evidence, accountability, equity, efficiency and fiscal responsibility as infrastructure. The claim that the benefits of social policies are not quantifiable should not stop ex ante appraisal, as methodologies exist to overcome this barrier.

An ex ante appraisal of a social project leaves an audit trail: the legislature, auditors, the media, and citizens can ask whether the project delivered what it promised. Many social schemes are implemented without the assessment of needs, identification of potential beneficiaries, or adequate funding, and a bureaucratic, top-down, target-chasing approach often replaces a democratic, bottom-up planning and implementation process.
This article explores the fiscal and economic fallout of cash transfers and universal subsidies.

If politics decides the desired social ends of such schemes, public finance and administration should decide the programme’s funding priority, the quantum of funding and the implementation process required to achieve those ends.

Prioritising expenditure is the first step in checking the desirability of public expenditure. For example, the Government of Tamil Nadu allocated nearly ₹1,000 crore in 2026-27 to provide scholarships for girls and boys from Government schools to continue higher education. A recent report in a Tamil Magazine ( Ananda Vikatan , November 18, 2026), based on replies it received to RTI applications, found 7,198 vacancies in permanent teaching positions in Government Arts and Science Colleges. If we include teacher vacancies in professional colleges and universities, the number should be nearly 9,000. Filling these vacancies, delayed for over a decade, would cost ₹1,080 crore per annum, rising every year thereafter. With a huge revenue deficit and fiscal deficit, the State budget lacks the revenue cushion to spend an additional ₹1,080 crore per annum. Prioritising is a normative decision: filling vacancies ensures students learn from regular teachers, whereas funding scholarships alone sends them to colleges without regular teachers.

Deciding the quantum of funding and the process of execution requires ex ante evaluation. This should be explicitly oriented toward designing programmes that maximise impact for a given cost, using behavioural models and micro-simulations to predict the effects of hypothetical programmes before implementation.

For instance, a universal subsidy scheme is a trade-off between inclusion and exclusion errors. If it is truly universal, the scheme commits the error of including the undeserving and thus reduces the per-capita benefit to people in need. In a target-oriented scheme, it commits the error of excluding the deserving, but it increases the per-capita benefit to people in need. The choice between the two requires ex ante appraisal of such schemes.

articles.title: Hackers breach U.S. Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so ⁠during work to upgrade the system, two people familiar with the matter said

Hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with ‌the matter told Reuters , in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, ​personnel and logistics data.

The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so ⁠during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.

In ‌a statement to Reuters , the Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the ‌Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities."

Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve ‌as ⁠a one-stop shop for the Air Force's IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, ⁠Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Among them are the Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defence radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions ​System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than ‌200 U.S. Air Force locations around the world.
SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2025, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force.
Cloud One is among the U.S. military's biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.
"A breach here ‌is a big deal," one of the sources said.
Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military's ​cyber force, to assess the damage, one of the sources said.

The discovery of the hack led to a ⁠range of disruption. Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused.

fullParagraphs: Tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended earlier this month after arsenic levels were found to be nearly 30 times government limits
As pollution mounts in its rivers, food and water, Thailand is pressing neighbouring Myanmar to tackle unregulated mining, while urging China to exert its influence in the war-ravaged nation.
Tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended earlier this month after arsenic levels were found to be nearly 30 times government limits.

Bangkok this week hosted the first Thai-Myanmar working group on the issue — also attended by the Chinese Ambassador — where it said tests proved rare-earth and gold mines in Myanmar were causing the pollution downstream. The two sides agreed to joint water sampling on the Kok and Sai rivers.

Bangkok is also looking to China, the main importer of rare-earth materials from Myanmar, to pressure private Chinese operators, as a months-long concern becomes increasingly urgent.

"Arsenic does not come from nature, it came from mining sites. The source was from (Myanmar's) Shan state, no-one disagrees," Science Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said. But how to tackle it remains an issue.

Thanapon Piman, senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), welcomed the agreement on joint sampling sites. "This is going to be a first step to agree on the evidence, otherwise you cannot move to the next step, like stopping mining activity," he told AFP . But Myanmar intervening to stop mining would be "really difficult", he added.

Multiple ethnic armed groups have been operating there for decades, while a 2021 military coup sparked an ongoing civil war. Thai officials pinpointed two gold mines just over the border from Mae Sai as the main source of high arsenic levels in the Sai River.

articles.title: Hasina has become a ‘thorn’ in Bangladesh-India ties: Minister Humaiun Kobir
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir says New Delhi is beginning to realise the strain the former Prime Minister’s presence in India is causing to bilateral relations

Sheikh Hasina has become a “thorn” in Bangladesh-India relations , with New Delhi beginning to realise the strain her presence in the country is causing to bilateral ties , State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir has said.

Comparing the deposed Prime Minister to an unwelcome guest who suddenly walks into someone’s home, Mr. Kobir said India was in a difficult position as it could neither send her away nor avoid dealing with her presence, news portal bdnews24 reported.
Read more: Sheikh Hasina’s return gambit tests Bangladesh’s political fault lines
“Hasina has become a thorn in Bangladesh-India relations ,” he told reporters at the Foreign Ministry on Thursday (November 26, 2026).
“She has become an irritation, and they understand that this is a problem for the relationship,” Mr. Kobir said.
His remarks came a day after India refrained from commenting on Ms. Hasina’s plan to return to Bangladesh on December 16.

External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) said that her voluntary return should be treated separately from Dhaka’s extradition request, which New Delhi was examining through established legal processes.
Mr. Kobir reiterated that Ms. Hasina could return only under the extradition treaty between India and Bangladesh, either in handcuffs or under strict surveillance.

“She is a criminal. There is one policy for criminals and another for ordinary citizens. She falls under the criminal category. She will come only through the extradition treaty. It is not a matter of her returning; she will be handed over,” he said.
Ms. Hasina’s presence in India has emerged as a contentious issue in bilateral ties since her departure from Bangladesh.

fullParagraphs: The talks in Islamabad will focus on West Asia and the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, two security officials said, with Pakistan’s Defence and Foreign Ministers and army chief attending

Pakistan is set to host talks with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Friday (November 27, 2026) under a trilateral defence pact that treats an attack on any member as an attack on all three, two security officials said.

The talks in Islamabad will focus on developments in West Asia, including ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels , the officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the meeting publicly.

Pakistan has said that the agreement is purely defensive in nature and not against anyone, including Iran, and that the trilateral alliance reflects a shared desire to strengthen strategic security cooperation.

Senior diplomats as well as defence and military officials from the three countries are expected to discuss ways to deter threats, expand military cooperation, share intelligence and strengthen defence industry ties, the officials said. Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif, Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir will attend the meeting.
Mr. Asif has said that Pakistan will use “whatever means are available” to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks from the Houthis.

However, Pakistan is still making efforts, with help from countries in West Asia, including Qatar, to urge the United States and Iran to return to the negotiating table to end the conflict in the region and beyond through talks. Pakistan had brokered an interim deal between the two sides in June 2026.

Friday’s meeting of the Strategic, Political and Defense Committee falls under the Joint Mecca Defense Agreement, which was signed in August 2026 in the Saudi holy city of Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

Pakistan’s government has not released details ahead of the meeting, but the authorities have declared a local holiday in Islamabad to limit public movement as part of security measures for the gathering. Islamabad traffic police have announced road diversions and advised motorists to use alternative routes to accommodate the movement of foreign delegations.

During a previous meeting in Riyadh, the three sides had vowed to immediately implement what they said were their collective defence commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed-upon military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.

According to the agreement, the group’s secretariat has been established in Saudi Arabia, and retired Pakistani General Nauman Mahmood has been selected as its first secretary-general. He will also attend Friday’s meeting. The pact binds the parties for 10 years, after which they would need to give three months’ notice before leaving.

articles.title: Costa Rica bars entry to UN rapporteur over ‘links to terrorist acts’
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Francesca Albanese arrived at the airport serving the capital, San Jose, to receive an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica, a public university

Costa Rica's government said on Thursday (November 26, 2026) it had denied entry to UN rapporteur Francesca Albanese, who has accused Israel of genocide, because she was the subject of an "international alert over links to terrorist acts."

Ms. Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, arrived on Thursday (November 26) at the airport serving the capital, San Jose, to receive an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica, a public university.

Ms. Albanese "is the subject of an international alert over links to terrorist acts," Omer Badilla, director general of Costa Rica's immigration authority, which falls under the interior ministry, said in a video posted on social media.
"I hope this clears up any doubts and makes clear the threat this woman poses to national security," he added.

The rector's office at the institution, the country's most important and prestigious university, said in a statement that immigration authorities were "blocking" Ms. Albanese's entry and asked the government to explain the decision.
The government of Costa Rican President Laura Fernández is a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump and has pursued closer trade ties with Israel since she took office in May.

Last December, Ms. Albanese criticised a free trade agreement between Costa Rica and Israel and called for its ratification to be put on hold, prompting a rebuke from the government, which accused her of interfering in domestic affairs.
The United States, Israel's main ally, imposed sanctions on Ms. Albanese after she criticised Washington's policy on Gaza.
"You see the face of empire the day you touch a nerve or cross its boundaries," Ms. Albanese wrote from the airport.

The university said it was awarding the honorary doctorate, which it grants annually to a prominent figure, in recognition of her "solid academic background, experience, publications and work exposing wrongdoing."

articles.title: Canada’s top court rules on Quebec secularism law in landmark case
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The law has been the subject of intense legal debate since it was first passed by Quebec's government in 2019
The Supreme Court rules on Friday (November 27, 2026) on one of Canada's most closely watched cases -- a Quebec law barring some provincial employees from wearing religious symbols.
The law has been the subject of intense legal debate since it was first passed by Quebec's government in 2019.

That is partly due to the implications for Quebec, a majority French-speaking province where the decades-long battle to enforce secularism is a core issue and where the Catholic Church once wielded enormous influence over public life.

The case reflects a conflict playing out elsewhere in the world as strictly secular states such as that of France face pressure typical of the Anglo-Saxon world for people to be able to practice their religion freely, including wearing whatever symbols of it that they wish.
The Quebec case is also seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the so-called "notwithstanding clause."
That clause, a quirk of Canada's legal system, effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution, known as the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Quebec pre-emptively invoked the "notwithstanding clause" when passing its secularism bill, anticipating it would be challenged over constitutional protections guaranteeing freedom of religion and expression.
Conservative-led provinces have also invoked the clause to defend legislation relating to transgender youth.
In 2023, Saskatchewan used the clause to pass a law requiring schools to obtain parental consent before changing the pronouns used for children under 16.
Alberta has also invoked the clause in relation to laws banning transgender girls from participating in female sports and restricting hormone therapy for individuals under 16.

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The Supreme Court rules on Friday (November 27, 2026) on one of Canada's most closely watched cases -- a Quebec law barring some provincial employees from wearing religious symbols.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Alberta has also invoked the clause in relation to laws banning transgender girls from participating in female sports and restricting hormone therapy for individuals under 16.

The Supreme Court rules on Friday (November 27, 2026) on one of Canada's most closely watched cases -- a Quebec law barring some provincial employees from wearing religious symbols.

The law has been the subject of intense legal debate since it was first passed by Quebec's government in 2019.

That is partly due to the implications for Quebec, a majority French-speaking province where the decades-long battle to enforce secularism is a core issue and where the Catholic Church once wielded enormous influence over public life.

The case reflects a conflict playing out elsewhere in the world as strictly secular states such as that of France face pressure typical of the Anglo-Saxon world for people to be able to practice their religion freely, including wearing whatever symbols of it that they wish.

The Quebec case is also seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the so-called "notwithstanding clause."

That clause, a quirk of Canada's legal system, effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution, known as the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Quebec pre-emptively invoked the "notwithstanding clause" when passing its secularism bill, anticipating it would be challenged over constitutional protections guaranteeing freedom of religion and expression.

Conservative-led provinces have also invoked the clause to defend legislation relating to transgender youth.

In 2023, Saskatchewan used the clause to pass a law requiring schools to obtain parental consent before changing the pronouns used for children under 16.

Alberta has also invoked the clause in relation to laws banning transgender girls from participating in female sports and restricting hormone therapy for individuals under 16.

articles.title: COP31: India welcomes $50 million climate fund pledge, says adaptation needs far greater
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: India has welcomed a $50 million pledge to the Adaptation Fund at the UN climate change conference COP31 , but said the contribution was inadequate given the scale of adaptation needs in developing countries and stressed that financial pledges must translate into timely and accessible resources.

In a written interview with PTI , Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav said the removal of the $120 billion adaptation finance figure from the proposed cover text, and the failure to reach an overarching agreement at COP31, were disappointing.

“The absence of an agreed formulation on the $120 billion adaptation finance figure in the final outcome is disappointing. It reflects the continuing difficulties in securing predictable financial commitments and agreement on how progress towards the existing goal of tripling adaptation finance by 2035 should be measured and monitored,” he said.

Mr. Yadav, however, noted that the absence of a cover decision did not extinguish developed countries’ commitments under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement.

He said adaptation was not a secondary consideration but an immediate developmental necessity for millions of vulnerable people. India had consistently maintained that adaptation finance must be adequate, predictable, primarily public and substantially grant-based, he added.

“Developing countries should not be compelled to incur additional debt to protect vulnerable communities from climate impacts. At COP31, India worked closely with Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) and G77 (largest bloc of 134 developing nations plus China) partners to seek stronger outcomes on adaptation finance and implementation support,” Yadav said.

He said India would continue to push for enhanced financial support, transparency in delivery and implementation of existing commitments, particularly for the poorest and most climate-vulnerable countries.

Mr. Yadav said that the failure to reach consensus on the proposed overarching agreement, the Antalya Pact, should not overshadow progress made on other issues and that the nation continues to deliver substantial climate action through its domestic efforts and resources.

“India engaged constructively throughout the Conference, working closely with BASIC, Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDCs) and G77 to secure a balanced and equitable outcome. We regret that consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact could not be reached. However, this should not overshadow the substantive progress achieved on several important issues,” he said.

On procedural decisions at COP31, Mr. Yadav said the Climate Finance Work Programme decision had established a process for further discussions, while the outcome on the Just Transition Work Programme was more substantive.

articles.title: MGM Healthcare Malar launches AI-powered MRI facility in Chennai
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: According to the hospital, the technology can reduce scan time; a brain MRI that conventionally takes about 35 minutes can now be completed in under 14 minutes
MGM Healthcare Malar, Adyar, has launched an AI-powered MRI facility, offering specialised imaging services for neurological, cardiac, musculoskeletal, spinal, and other conditions.
The facility was inaugurated by J. Radhakrishnan, Chairperson of the Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission, on Thursday (November 26, 2026).

The system uses deep learning algorithms to correct motion-related artefacts and improve image quality, potentially reducing the need for repeat scans. It also offers specialised fetal and breast MRI, cardiac MRI, whole-body imaging, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and perfusion imaging.

According to the hospital, the technology can also reduce scan time. A brain MRI that conventionally takes about 35 minutes can now be completed in under 14 minutes. This could benefit patients who find it difficult to remain still for prolonged periods due to pain or discomfort.

Thinesh Ram, senior consultant and head of Imaging and Interventional Radiology, MGM Healthcare Malar, said the system would enable more detailed evaluation of neural pathways and expand the range of diagnostic assessments.

S. Kripanandh, chief operating officer, MGM Healthcare Malar, Adyar, and group chief business officer, said the facility would strengthen the hospital’s diagnostic capabilities and expand access to advanced imaging services in the neighbourhood.

articles.title: Elevated blood sugar during adulthood linked with worse cognition in midlife: study
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The findings suggest that changes in glucose metabolism may affect brain health earlier in adulthood than previously thought

Young adults with progressively increasing fasting blood sugar may be more likely to have a poor cognitive functioning by midlife, according to a new study that tracked young adults for over three decades.
The findings suggest that changes in glucose metabolism may affect brain health earlier in adulthood than previously thought.
Participants who developed type 2 diabetes during the study also showed signs of structural brain changes, according to findings published in the Journal of the American Heart Association .

"Diabetes is known to affect cognitive function, but cognitive impairment due to diabetes was once believed to happen mostly during childhood among people with Type 1 diabetes or after age 65 in people with Type 2 diabetes," lead author Regina Paradela, a post-doctoral researcher at the University of São Paulo Medical School in São Paulo, Brazil, said.

"However, prediabetes and sustained elevated fasting blood sugar levels in adults without type 1 or type 2 diabetes may also have an increased risk of late-life cognitive decline and dementia," Paradela said.
The researchers suggested early monitoring and management of blood sugar levels in young adulthood -- 18 to 30 years old -- might be a strategy to preserve brain health.

Normal fasting blood glucose is generally below 100 milligrams per decilitre, 100-125 milligrams per decilitre indicates prediabetes and a value over 126 milligrams per decilitre is consistent with Type 2 diabetes.

"The fact that increasing glucose levels were associated with poorer cognitive performance, even among people who had not developed Type 2 diabetes during the 30-year study, is very important," Paradela said.
"This suggests that changes in glucose metabolism may be relevant to brain health earlier in adulthood than we typically think about," Paradela said.

The study is among the first to investigate and compare the association between changes in fasting blood sugar levels from early adulthood to changes in cognition and brain structure in middle age, over approximately 30 years, the researchers said.

articles.title: Parenting in an anxious age: What does ‘good enough’ look like?
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: In a time of global tension, digital overload and endless advice about raising children, experts say 2027 calls for a radical rethink: less perfection, more presence

Prem Kishore occasionally turns to Artificial Intelligence (AI) for help when it comes to raising his six-year-old son. “It’s the big feelings that can be difficult to talk about, because we don’t always have the right words. I usually seek advice from my friends or psychologists, but if they’re not available, I turn to AI,” says the creative professional, 43, who splits his time between Bengaluru and Dubai.
Kishore recalls how he visited an AI video generator to create an avatar of a doctor, who chatted with his son about healthy boundaries and consent.

As AI becomes more enmeshed in our day-to-day lives, families are turning to it for advice, research and assistance in managing the mental load of modern-day parenting. A 2026 consumer trends report by GIPSI, the research arm of agency Tonic Worldwide, combined search and social media data with a survey of 50,000 people, and found that 52% of Indian Gen Z parents now use AI instead of their usual search engines, and 48% use it as an adviser. In India, Google Gemini recently launched a series of commercials featuring Shah Rukh Khan in which he directs two fathers at very different stages of their parenting journeys towards the chatbot for advice. Apps such as Fambot and AVA seek to help families with administrative tasks by syncing to their calendars, email and online shopping orders.

Eighteen years ago, when I first became a parent, Dr. Spock’s Baby and Child Care was the de facto gift to all new parents along with a Johnson & Johnson baby care set. I kept the book for a number of years after I had my second child and referred to it frequently. But today, new parents can seek advice from podcasts, influencers, online communities and yes, AI chatbots. There is a lot of advice out there, available in seconds. But how much of it is actually helping parents?

Author-editor Sanjana Kapur, 40, who’s raising a nine-year-old in Bengaluru, admits that parenting feels a little nerve-racking today. “There’s so much information out there, that you’re constantly worrying if you’re making the right decision, or how even your smallest reaction will affect your child. The world has become such a complicated place, and parents are nervous even when kids are at school now,” she admits.

articles.title: Lifting off: on China’s launch of Pakistan’s first astronaut
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Science-based diplomacy could aid India-Pakistan bilateral engagement

The economic and diplomatic consequences of India’s efforts to estrange Pakistan often overshadow the costs distributed between them. For example, Pakistani space scientists can today access facilities in China whereas Indian space scientists can access facilities in the United States and Europe . But Indian scientists studying environmental conditions in Pakistan and Pakistani scientists studying conditions in India have far fewer alternatives. The latter matters much more for regional development and stability. On November 25, Beijing’s ‘Space Silk Road’ diplomacy and the strain on New Delhi’s hedging strategies converged in the Shenzhou-24 mission as China launched Pakistan’s first astronaut , Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, to the Tiangong space station. Pakistan had offered in 2015 to contribute to India’s proposed SAARC satellite and wanted the project administered under SAARC, but India insisted on operating it as largesse to its neighbours. If it had really been SAARC’s satellite, ISRO and its Pakistani counterpart, SUPARCO , could have developed an institutional relationship and India could have influenced its neighbour’s space programme through a multilateral mechanism. But today, India’s ability to engage Pakistan on regional matters has increasingly depended on negotiating with powers beyond South Asia, in institutions with other agendas.

Even as spaceflight emerges as a new geopolitical realm, its substantial scientific component affords countries opportunities to engage independently of interstate relations in other domains. The Shenzhou-24 experience will be significant for SUPARCO just as the Axiom-4 mission in the U.S. was for ISRO , helping to significantly lower Islamabad’s cost to access similar future opportunities, especially those under the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization, which also includes Bangladesh, and the Belt and Road Initiative’s Space Information Corridor . There is no question that Indian spaceflight is technologically superior to that of Pakistan, but the Shenzhou-24 mission is a reminder that China’s technological superiority vis-à-vis India’s leaves India with an unequal contest. India has been ceding the neighbourhood to China’s space networks, and by squandering the opportunities afforded by science diplomacy, it has left Pakistan to look to China even on problems it shares with India. The Apollo-Soyuz interaction during the Cold War and India and Pakistan working together to respond to a locust outbreak barely a year after the Balakot crisis (2019) are testament to the ability of science-based diplomacy to clear room for bilateral engagement with guardrails, without compromising the counter-terrorism agenda. India should revive such engagement.

There is no question that Indian spaceflight is technologically superior to that of Pakistan, but the Shenzhou-24 mission is a reminder that China’s technological superiority vis-à-vis India’s leaves India with an unequal contest. India has been ceding the neighbourhood to China’s space networks, and by squandering the opportunities afforded by science diplomacy, it has left Pakistan to look to China even on problems it shares with India. The Apollo-Soyuz interaction during the Cold War and India and Pakistan working together to respond to a locust outbreak barely a year after the Balakot crisis (2019) are testament to the ability of science-based diplomacy to clear room for bilateral engagement with guardrails, without compromising the counter-terrorism agenda. India should revive such engagement.

articles.title: RBI cuts daily CRR maintenance to 90%, to unlock over ₹40,000 crore
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The latest relaxation is expected to improve banks’ liquidity flexibility and support credit deployment.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Friday eased the minimum daily maintenance requirement for the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99% to 90%, a move expected to release more than ₹40,000 crore into the banking system and provide banks with additional funds for lending.

“On the basis of an assessment of the current and evolving macroeconomic situation and liquidity conditions, it has been decided to reduce the minimum daily maintenance of the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99% of the requirement to 90% effective from the fortnight beginning December 1, 2026,” the RBI said.

Under the revised arrangement, scheduled banks will be required to maintain at least 90% of their prescribed CRR on each day of the reporting fortnight. However, the average daily CRR maintained during the fortnight must not fall below the level prescribed by the RBI.

With the prescribed CRR currently at 3% of a bank’s net demand and time liabilities (NDTL), banks will now have greater flexibility in managing their daily cash balances, while continuing to meet the overall fortnightly requirement.

The latest move reverses the tightening introduced on October 9, shortly after the previous Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting. At the time, the RBI had raised the minimum daily CRR maintenance requirement from 90% to 99%, effective from the fortnight beginning October 16, 2026.
The earlier move came when the banking system was flush with liquidity following substantial mobilisation of funds through foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits.

articles.title: Chinese Military tests new Taiwan landing tactics in coastal drills
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The exercise in Dacheng Bay was first spotted on November 1, according to a report by geospatial data company ingeniSPACE reviewed by Reuters

China is staging a weeks-long amphibious landing drill in the province facing Taiwan, testing a new method to land troops ashore by linking civilian vessels ‌into a makeshift floating bridge, satellite images and a research report showed.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as ​its own territory, despite Taipei's rejection of Beijing's sovereignty claims, and has never renounced the use of force to ⁠bring it under Chinese control.

The exercise, in Dacheng Bay in China's southeastern province of Fujian, was first spotted on November 1, according to satellite images and a report by geospatial data company ingeniSPACE reviewed by Reuters.

"The People's Liberation Army appeared to be rehearsing low-signature methods to provide logistical support ‌to forces that could be involved in a first island chain invasion scenario," said Jason Wang, the company's chief operating officer.
"Using civilian ships to enable bridging of heavy equipment and materiel from deeper waters creates additional locations they can use ‌along the Taiwan coastline."

A senior security official briefed on the drill in Dacheng Bay, just 280 km (175 miles) from ‌Taiwan's ⁠main island, confirmed it was still in progress on Friday, but made no direct link to local elections ⁠set for the next day.

Analysis of the images from November 1 to 16 showed the vessels manoeuvred around the bay, forming and dismantling a floating bridge about 800 m (2,600 ft) long, in activity also seen in images from commercial providers Vantor and Planet Labs.

Eight civilian vessels participated, made up ​of four barges, two semi-submersible and two powered, along with ‌four landing craft, as well as smaller support vessels and Chinese navy ships nearby, ingeniSPACE's analysis and tracking data showed.

No purpose-built bridging equipment was observed, suggesting China's military may be honing its use of existing civilian maritime resources to improvise landing infrastructure in a combat scenario, ingeniSPACE said.
The senior security official confirmed the report details.

articles.title: Saudi strike kills 11 in Yemen, reports Houthi media
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The latest incidents came a day after a deadly Houthi attack on a Saudi oil refinery, and add to a growing tally of violence since Yemen's civil war reignited over the summer
A Saudi strike killed 11 people on Friday (November 27, 2026) in Yemen, Houthi media said, as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it shot down a drone targeting Riyadh.
The latest incidents came a day after a deadly Houthi attack on a Saudi oil refinery, and add to a growing tally of violence since Yemen's civil war reignited over the summer.
The coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government against the Iran-allied Houthis, has been regularly bombing areas under their control.
Ukraine says it struck two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region
In response, Houthi forces have been targeting the oil-rich kingdom almost daily, hitting energy facilities, airports and the financial district of the capital, Riyadh.

Saudi warplanes carried out a raid on a residential building in the city of Al-Turba in Taiz governorate on Friday, killing "11 citizens, most of them children", the Houthis' Saba news agency said, citing a local source.
The agency also reported strikes targeting fuel tanks in the Saada region, the movement's birthplace and stronghold.

On Thursday (November 26, 2026), the Houthis targeted the Jazan refinery in southern Saudi Arabia, killing a Nepalese worker and injuring several other people, according to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
The attack also triggered a fire that led to the shutdown of the facility, SPA said.
Yemen plunged back into war in July, after years of relative calm, opening a new front in the West Asia war.

articles.title: Hyderabad’s air pollution puts focus on hospitals; doctors call for city-level health database
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Hospitals want to share anonymised data on respiratory illnesses, strokes and cardiovascular conditions, while doctors propose using daily AQI readings to alert vulnerable patients

With Hyderabad recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of over 300 on Deepavali and many other days recording poor air quality earlier this year, doctors and public health experts have called for a coordinated effort by hospitals to track the health effects of pollution and build a city-level database that can help shape public policy.

The issue came into focus during a panel discussion on ‘Impact of Mobility on Air Quality and Public Health’ at Cyberabad Moves, where doctors said that the effects of polluted air went beyond respiratory illnesses and were also linked to cardiovascular problems and strokes. They stressed that the health consequences of daily exposure to pollution, particularly during commutes, needed to be documented through local medical data.

Pawan Mukulutla of WRI India, who moderated the discussion, pointed out that congestion was only the most visible consequence of the way people travelled. The less visible costs included exposure to polluted air, unsafe roads and the lack of pedestrian infrastructure. He cited Hyderabad’s AQI crossing 300 on Deepavali and said particulate matter levels, including PM2.5 and PM10, had been several times above prescribed thresholds.

Dr. Sudheer Vinnamala, Regional Medical Director of KIMS, said hospitals could work together to create a Hyderabad-level health database by sharing anonymised information on respiratory illnesses, strokes and cardiovascular conditions with public health authorities.

“What you can’t measure, you can’t manage,” he said, arguing that such a database could help identify vulnerable groups and establish a clearer picture of the relationship between air quality and health outcomes.

He said doctors could also use daily AQI information to alert patients with asthma and other respiratory conditions when pollution levels deteriorated, allowing them to take precautions and avoid unnecessary exposure. Hospitals could play a role in reducing pollution and traffic by encouraging carpooling, staggering appointments and arranging last-mile transport links from Metro stations.

Dr Vishwanath Gella, a pulmonologist at AIG Hospitals, said pollution affected people with and without pre-existing health conditions. He said doctors were seeing patients with asthma, respiratory infections and other lung-related complaints, with an increase in cases during periods of poor air quality, particularly around Deepavali and in winter.

Dr Shailaja Tetali of the Public Health Foundation of India said research into school travel patterns showed that around 80 per cent of children lived within two to three kilometres of their schools. A majority travelled by public transport, walked or cycled.

While walking and cycling offered physical activity, children using these modes were also exposed to roadside pollution and faced road safety risks. She said improving infrastructure around schools could address several of these concerns, as interventions within a three-kilometre radius could cover a large proportion of children’s daily journeys.

She called for authorities to act on existing evidence instead of repeatedly commissioning studies, suggesting that interventions could first be tested in smaller areas and then replicated across the city.

articles.title: Robotic technology can improve precision and recovery in knee replacement, say experts
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The webinar discussed the role of robotics in improving surgical precision, implant positioning and recovery in total knee replacement

The Hindu , in association with Kauvery Hospital, conducted a webinar on Friday titled ‘The Role of Robotics in Knee Replacement’. Orthopaedic specialists discussed the use of robotic-assisted technology in total knee replacement (TKR), its benefits, post-operative recovery, costs and the role of surgeons in performing the procedure.

The experts were Mukunth K., senior consultant, orthopaedic surgeon, joint replacement and sports injuries, Kauvery Hospital, Alwarpet; P.R. Ramasamy, head of the department of orthopaedics and pelviacetabular and joint replacement surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Tiruchi; and Manivannan, consultant, orthopaedics, arthroscopy and joint replacement surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Salem.

Dr. Mukunth explained how robotic-assisted technology helps surgeons plan knee replacement procedures through bone mapping, precise measurements and real-time guidance. He said the technology helped surgeons make accurate bone cuts and position implants closer to the intended alignment. He compared the robot’s role to GPS navigation, emphasising that the surgeon remained in control of the procedure.

He said manual measurements during conventional surgery could vary by 2–3 mm, even in experienced hands. Greater precision in bone cuts and implant alignment could help reduce soft-tissue trauma and blood loss during surgery and improve post-operative outcomes.

Dr. Ramasamy explained the steps involved in robotic-assisted knee replacement. He said the procedure involved less damage to the surrounding bone, which could make a future revision surgery easier. articles.title: All to play for: On the World chess championship in Geneva
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Chess is one sport where both the young and the old can excel

The World chess championship opened in Geneva with a game worthy of the occasion. Both the defending champion, D. Gukesh, and his challenger, Javokhir Sindarov, produced chess of top quality, and the draw was a just result . Given that the Indian was playing with black pieces and that he had gone into the match as the less favoured of the two, Gukesh could be a little happier with the game than his Uzbek rival. The Chennai Grandmaster was in considerable time trouble on multiple occasions, but managed to solve his problems and found proper answers to the questions posed to him on the board by the confident Sindarov. The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival.

Sindarov is just six months older than Gukesh, making the Geneva match the youngest in the 140-year-old history of the World championship: both players are 20. It is remarkable that Gukesh has already seen the highs and lows of life at such a young age. For his opponent, the last one year has been better than a dream: from World No. 26 he has risen to No. 4. Chess is getting younger. The next World championship could also very well have two young contenders. Grandmasters are usually said to peak when they are around 30 and chess is one game that even older players have continued to excel in. Viswanathan Anand was 48 when he won the World rapid chess championship . The match between Gukesh and Sindarov has attracted considerable interest from across the sporting world. After the 1972 match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer — the defining moment of world chess — the World championship has earned a reputation as one of the planet’s most important sporting events. No battle between two of the world’s most talented men in chess has ever disappointed.

articles.title: India, China hold high-level talks in Arunachal sector on border management, LAC issues: MEA
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: MEA spokesperson Randhir also addressed a report claiming China-sourced satellite data may have aided Pakistan in tracking Indian troop movements and monitoring installations during Operation Sindoor

The Indian and Chinese armies held high-level talks this month in the Arunachal Pradesh sector focusing on border management and addressing outstanding issues along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

The talks, believed to have spread over a number of days , were held amid reports of aggressive military posturing by Chinese troops along the frontier, especially in the Upper Subansiri region of Arunachal Pradesh.
In September too, the senior military commanders of the two armies were engaged in flag talks in two sessions on both sides of the frontier in the Arunachal Pradesh sector.

“India and China engage regularly through diplomatic and military mechanisms and you are well aware of those mechanisms,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at his regular media briefing while responding to a question.

“A meeting of the senior military commanders was held in the eastern sector recently. Discussions between the two sides focused on improving border management as well as addressing outstanding issues along the LAC,” he said.
Mr. Jaiswal said such interactions are aimed at maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas and preventing any escalation.
Locations of two additional India-China border meeting points yet to be announced

Lt. Gen Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Army’s III Corps headquartered near Dimapur in Nagaland, led the Indian delegation at the talks in the second week of this month, while the Chinese side was led by his counterpart.

In the military and diplomatic talks, India has been conveying to the Chinese side the importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity in the frontier regions for the continued development and progress of the overall bilateral relationship.

In the last one-and-a-half years, the two sides have taken a series of measures to rebuild their relationship after it came under severe strain following the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in eastern Ladakh in 2020.
